extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning basic combinatorics and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter on elementary counting: permutations, combinations, Pascal's triangle/binomial theorem, inclusion–exclusion, stars-and-bars, multisets, and pigeonhole/division principles with worked examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficient formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For integers n,k with 0 < k < n, the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set is (n choose k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!). (For the edge cases k = 0 or k = n the value is 1.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to count k-element subsets (combinations) such as 4-element subsets of a 9-element set (Example 3.11). The text shows algebraic manipulations and small worked computations (e.g. (9 choose 4)=126).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation count P(n,k)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of k-permutations (ordered lists of k distinct elements) from an n-element set is P(n,k) = n! / (n-k)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reason about arranging subsets into ordered lists (e.g., table method that lists all 3-permutations of {a,b,c,d,e} and relates P(5,3) to 3! times number of 3-element subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a procedure is performed in stages and stage i has a_i possible outcomes independent of other stages, then the total number of outcomes is the product ∏ a_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to multi-step selection problems: e.g., choose 2 evens (C(4,2)=6) and 3 odds (C(5,3)=10) then multiply to get 60 5-element subsets with exactly two even elements (Example 3.12). Also used to count lists formed from independent choices (cards of suits, separate choices for clubs and hearts in Example 3.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition Principle (disjoint union)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set can be partitioned into disjoint parts, the size of the whole is the sum of the sizes of the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when breaking a counting task into mutually exclusive cases; e.g., decomposing the set of binary strings with odd number of 1's into sets with 1,3,5,7 ones and summing their sizes (Example 3.16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-set Inclusion–Exclusion (Fact 3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite sets A and B: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains correction for double-counting when sets overlap. Worked example: count 3-card hands that are all red or all face cards by computing |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| (Example 3.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-set Inclusion–Exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite sets A,B,C: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided with Venn diagram motivation and the general combinatorial reasoning; recommended for more complex union cardinality problems (Equation (3.5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial identity: C(n+1,k) = C(n,k) + C(n,k-1) for integers n,k with 1 < k < n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial proof: count k-element subsets of {0,1,...,n} by whether they contain 0 or not. This recursion generates Pascal's triangle (Figure 3.3) and underlies the triangle construction rule: each entry is sum of two above it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry of binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains row symmetry in Pascal's triangle (exercise references). Useful identity for simplifying combinatorial expressions and computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial Theorem (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-negative integer n: (x + y)^n = Σ_{k=0}^n C(n,k) x^{n−k} y^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to expand binomials (examples: expansion of (x+y)^7 and (a−b)^4). The text states the theorem (to be proved later) and shows practical use for coefficient extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stars-and-bars encoding for multisets
rubrics_metrics.description: Any k-element multiset formed from an n-element set can be encoded as a list with k stars and n−1 bars (a bar separating each element type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding transforms multiset counting into choosing positions for bars (or stars) in a length k + n − 1 list; demonstrated via tables and examples (encoding multisets from {a,b,c,d}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiset count formula (Fact 3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of k-element multisets from an n-element set is C(n + k − 1, k) (equivalently C(n + k − 1, n − 1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived via stars-and-bars encoding. Examples: number of 5-element multisets from 4 symbols is C(8,5)=56; number of 20-element multisets from 3 symbols is C(22,20)=231 (Example 3.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model integer solutions via multisets / stars-and-bars
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of non-negative integer solutions to x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_n = k equals C(n + k − 1, k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret a solution as a k-element multiset on n symbols or as stars-and-bars with k stars and n−1 bars. Example: w+x+y+z=20 has C(23,3)=1771 solutions (Example 3.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutations of a multiset (Fact 3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a multiset has total size n with multiplicities p1,p2,...,pr, then the number of distinct permutations (arrangements) is n! / (p1! p2! ... pr!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via treating identical letters as distinguishable then dividing by internal permutations; examples include BANANA (6!/(3!2!1!)=60) and MISSISSIPPI (11!/(4!4!2!1!)=34,650).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division principle (Fact 3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed into k boxes, then at least one box contains ⌈n/k⌉ or more objects, and at least one box contains ⌊n/k⌋ or fewer objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by average; presents both upper- and lower-bound guarantees. Used to reason about distributions and extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole Principle (Fact 3.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed into k boxes: if n > k then some box contains more than one object; if n < k then some box is empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of the division principle; illustrated with examples like birthdays in months and guarantees about minima/maxima in groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction (complement) principle
rubrics_metrics.description: To count the number of outcomes not having a property, subtract the number that do have the property from the total number of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Example 3.18: count hands that are not (all red or all face cards) by subtracting the number that are from the total number of 3-card hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting binary strings with fixed number of ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of n-bit binary strings with exactly k ones equals C(n,k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to count binary-strings examples (e.g., 7-digit binary strings with odd number of ones by summing C(7,1)+C(7,3)+C(7,5)+C(7,7) in Example 3.16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling guidance: choose appropriate representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve counting problems by modeling them as one of: permutations (ordered, no repetition), combinations (unordered, no repetition), multisets/stars-and-bars (unordered, repetition allowed), binary-strings/position-selection, or unions/intersections for inclusion–exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the chapter problems are mapped to these canonical models: 5-card hands → 5-element subsets; club/heart splits → product of combinations; lottery tickets → combinations; distributions of identical objects → stars-and-bars; complement and union cases handled via subtraction and inclusion–exclusion.
